source.title: Pushing the right boundaries matters! Wasserstein Adversarial Training for Label Noise
source.authors: B. Damodaran; Kilian Fatras; Sylvain Lobry; Rémi Flamary; D. Tuia; N. Courty

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including the appendix. No relevant truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates test accuracy under several levels of simulated label noise, but uses class-dependent noise and does not report training error, so it tests only part of V4 with a different setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracies for CCE under 0%, 20%, and 40% class-dependent label noise. It does not report whether CCE fits the noisy training labels, and its noise is not completely random. Comparisons of WAR and other methods are not included as claim rows because they change the training method.
record.test_reason: The CCE baseline directly tests V4's test-performance component across increasing stochastic, class-dependent label corruption. It does not measure perfect training fit or extend corruption to 100%.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that WAR uses class similarities or prior knowledge to shape regularization and improves robustness to noisy labels across their benchmark and real-world classification and segmentation experiments.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates adversarial regularization methods for learning with noisy labels; its benchmark noise is class-dependent and its reported outcome is test accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different test accuracies across datasets and simulated noise rates; it also reports sensitivity to the regularization parameter β for WAR variants, outside the extracted CCE rows.
record.problems: For the claim-relevant CCE results, the paper reports test accuracy but not training error. Simulated noise is class-dependent, is tested only at 0%, 20%, and 40%, and is not completely random labeling.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional noisy-label test-accuracy results for WAR variants and competing methods in Tables 1–6 and 8. They are omitted because those methods alter the training procedure and do not measure fitting random labels by standard training.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters for that intervention.
Time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowing with increasing corruption. Reported timing compares training methods instead.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit, memorization of corrupted labels while capturing remaining signal, and degradation through corruption rates above 40% to chance. Uniform random corruption is not examined.
Whether weight decay, dropout or augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing these makes clean-label generalization poor.

Comparative learning trajectories establishing that shared real patterns are fitted before noisy labels. The appendix's qualitative observation of no early overfitting does not establish this ordering.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's limits_scope verdict: unreported training error and untested corruption rates are coverage gaps, not demonstrated failures. The reported noise rates are class-conditional flip probabilities; they need not equal the realized fraction of corrupted labels across the entire dataset. The study is not an original source for these versions.

versions.untested_parts: No result reports training error or fitting completely random labels, chance test error, or whether architecture and training hyperparameters were unchanged for that intervention.
No training-time comparison for fitting random versus true labels, or convergence rate across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.

Rows record the reported test-accuracy trend under 0%, 20%, and 40% class-dependent noise. The paper does not report training fit, completely random corruption, corruption rates above 40%, or whether the remaining signal is captured while noise is memorized.
Dropout and data augmentation appear in some training setups, but the paper does not test removing them or whether they prevent fitting random labels or affect generalization on true labels.
The paper cites Arpit et al. but does not report its own experiment on the order in which real and noisy labels are learned.

relationships.condition: CCE-trained 9-layer CNN on Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 0%, 20% and 40% asymmetric class-dependent noise; test-performance component only.
relationships.reason: Accuracy decreases at both noise increments on every dataset: 94.69→89.02→78.85%, 91.76→85.26→76.23%, and 68.60→58.81→42.45% (R1–R9).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy declined successively from 94.69% to 89.02% to 78.85% on Fashion-MNIST, 91.76% to 85.26% to 76.23% on CIFAR-10, and 68.60% to 58.81% to 42.45% on CIFAR-100.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CCE on Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 with simulated class-dependent noise at 0%, 20%, and 40%
reader_labels.reason: Test accuracy decreases at each reported increase in noise rate for all three datasets (R1–R9). This supports the test-degradation component in these settings.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The paper does not report training error and uses class-dependent noise only up to 40%, so these results do not establish perfect fitting under complete random corruption (R1–R9).
